cim: Explainable artificial intelligence for prehospital identification of endovascular thrombectomy candidates: a retrospective real-world study

cim_eredeti: Explainable artificial intelligence for prehospital identification of endovascular thrombectomy candidates: a retrospective real-world study

Acute ischaemic stroke due to large-vessel occlusion requires rapid endovascular treatment (EVT). Prehospital stroke scales, though widely used, have not achieved an optimal balance of sensitivity, specificity, and overall discriminative performance, underlining the need for evaluation of machine learning (ML) approaches to improve early identification of EVT candidates. We conducted a retrospective development and internal validation study based on digital real-world data from consecutive EMS-transported patients with suspected stroke (n = 1,435, 94 EVT events [6.6%]) from the Stroke Angel initiative in a rural region in Germany (Rhön-Grabfeld), covering the period from January 2015 to June 2021. Predicted probabilities of six ML models were recalibrated using Platt scaling, and clinical relevance was evaluated using decision curve analysis (DCA). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values were computed to quantify individual feature contributions to model predictions. Among 287 patients (24 EVT events) in the evaluation cohort, Random Forest achieved the highest AUROC (0.85 [95% CI, 0.78–0.90]), with sensitivity of 0.92 [0.74–0.99], specificity of 0.66 [0.60–0.72]. The 4I-SS (score > 2) yielded an AUROC of 0.82 [0.72–0.89], sensitivity of 0.87 [0.67–0.96], and specificity of 0.69 [0.64–0.74]. Bootstrapped intervals overlapped across all metrics and platt scaling probabilities, suggesting no statistically significant superiority.

Stroke is a major global health burden and ranks as the second leading cause of death worldwide1. Endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) is the standard of care for acute ischemic stroke with large-vessel occlusion (LVO), supported by high-quality randomized evidence and exceptionally low numbers needed to treat2. Acute stroke requires immediate identification of patients and their rapid transfer to comprehensive stroke centres for EVT3. However, in many stroke systems, stroke assessment does not commence until after hospital arrival, which slows down treatment. Delays could be avoided if emergency medical service (EMS) teams recognized LVO and its severity on scene, prioritize patients instantly, and route them directly to the centre that offers the fastest access to reperfusion therapy4,5.

Since only a minority of suspected stroke cases ultimately harbour a proximal LVO, routing all patients directly to a comprehensive stroke (“mothership”) centre may not always be practical or necessary, emphasizing the significance of effective prehospital allocation. Hospitals without EVT capability must expeditiously transfer such patients fast—ideally while thrombolysis continues—to the nearest comprehensive stroke centre with EVT capacity (“drip-and-ship”)6. The avoidance of treatment delays necessitates formalized agreements and predefined protocols between the referring hospital, the designated EVT centre, and the EMS7.

EVT is restricted to a highly selected subset of patients with acute ischemic stroke. In response, severity-based triage strategies commonly use a National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale threshold of ≥ 7 to increase the efficiency of patient selection for advanced imaging and endovascular pathways2. Conventional prehospital scales have been designed to detect LVO, yet this approach neglects the broader determinants of EVT8,9. Prehospital stroke scales, though widely used, have not achieved an optimal balance of sensitivity, specificity, and predictive value. Even prehospital stroke scales computed ex ante demonstrate performance comparable to manually derived scales and do not confer superior LVO-detection10. The decision to pursue EVT depends not only on vessel status but also on patient-specific and contextual factors that may not be captured by conventional scales.

Collecting structured prehospital data and reliably linking them to hospital-based outcome measures is challenging due to heterogeneous documentation workflows and limited interoperability across emergency and hospital information systems11.

Machine-learning (ML) approaches, by integrating multimodal prehospital and hospital data, has the potential to refine prehospital stroke triage, reduce transfers, and increase the likelihood that patients who stand to benefit from EVT reach comprehensive stroke centres faster12. These predictions may support prehospital decision-making and better inform paramedics or emergency physicians. Although real-world data (RWD) has been identified as a potential source of ML model development, its utilisation in this field remains scarce13.

The primary objective is to develop and internally validate ML models that estimate the likelihood of a patient undergoing EVT during the acute hospital admission based on prehospital and early in-hospital RWD. The secondary objective is to assess the calibration of predicted probabilities and to evaluate the impact of classification thresholds on prehospital triage decisions, particularly the balance between over- and undertriage. The models are embedded within an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) framework to enable interpretation of model outputs and decision logic. This study is designed as a proof of concept for data-driven prehospital EVT triage and aims to explore the potential clinical utility of an explainable decision-support approach.

A total of 3,628 records from Database A (prehospital) and 5,975 records from Database B (hospital) were extracted. After excluding records without valid timestamps, non-EMS missions and records outside the study period, 3,659 hospital EMS admissions remained. Of the linked candidate pairs, 2,195 records were excluded because they failed the eligibility check, defined as a timestamp discrepancy of more than 60 min or an age difference of more than one year between prehospital and hospital record. Record linkage identified 1,464 matched records. Of these, 29 duplicate index entries were removed, yielding 1,435 unique linked patients comprising the preprocessed data set. Transport mode and admission pathway inclusion criteria were applied prior to linkage to ensure cohort comparability. The final cohort was randomly partitioned into training (n = 918), validation (n = 230), and test sets (n = 287). Among included patients, 94 (6.6%) underwent EVT and 356 (24.8%) received IVT. With 1,148 patients and 70 EVT events, this cohort fell short of the calculated target, increasing the risk of overfitting (Fig. 1).
